# testdata

Fixtures captured from real hardware on 2026-09-14. Everything here was
produced by the actual Pimoroni library talking to our actual board, so these
are **oracles, not guesses**. If your code disagrees with a fixture, your code
is wrong.

Regenerate with `tools/` — see §4.

---

## 1. `eeprom/` — identification records

29-byte records, little-endian, layout `<HHBBB22p`:

```
offset  size  field
0       2     width           uint16
2       2     height          uint16
4       1     colour          uint8   index into the colour table
5       1     pcbVariant      uint8   STORED x10 — 100 means board v10.0
6       1     displayVariant  uint8   index into the variant table
7       1     writeTime len   uint8   Pascal string length
8       21    writeTime       ASCII
```

| File | Content | A correct parser must |
|---|---|---|
| `what-jd79668.bin` | **The real board.** `400x300`, colour 7 (`red/yellow`), pcb 100 (`v10.0`), variant 24 (`Red/Yellow wHAT (JD79668)`), written `2025-08-20 15:51:55.5` | decode all six fields exactly |
| `truncated.bin` | 12 bytes — a short read | return an error, **not** a zero-valued struct |
| `zeroed.bin` | 29 × `0x00` — no EEPROM present | error: geometry `0x0` is impossible |
| `ones.bin` | 29 × `0xFF` — floating bus, nothing ACKing | error: geometry `65535x65535` is impossible |
| `unknown-variant.bin` | valid, but `displayVariant = 254` | error naming the unknown variant; must not index past the table |
| `zero-geometry.bin` | valid variant, `0x0` dimensions | error |
| `empty-writetime.bin` | valid, Pascal length `0` | succeed, with `WriteTime == ""` |

The last three exist because each corresponds to a plausible parser bug:
out-of-range slice index, accepting nonsense geometry, and mishandling an empty
Pascal string.

### Why `pcbVariant` is divided by ten

The EEPROM stores `100` for board revision `10.0`. The vendor library divides by
10 without comment. Ours should divide *and say why*.

---

## 2. `conformance/` — the rendering and packing oracle

A deterministic 400×300 pattern. **Every pixel is a pure function of its
coordinates** — no fonts, no randomness, no timestamps.

| File | Size | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `conformance.idx` | 120,000 B | one palette index per pixel, row-major from (0,0) |
| `conformance.bin` | 30,000 B | the packed framebuffer the vendor library sends to the panel |
| `conformance.png` | — | what it should look like |

### Why there is no text in it

Pillow and Go's `x/image/font` rasterise glyphs differently — different hinting,
different rounding. A text-bearing image can therefore **never** be compared
byte-for-byte between the Python reference and a Go port. Keeping this pattern
font-free is what makes an exact comparison possible at all.

Test text separately, against golden PNGs generated by our own Go code.

### What the bands test

| Rows | Tests |
|---|---|
| 0–39 | flat fills of all four inks, 100px columns |
| 40–99 | 1px horizontal rules at pitch 2, 3, 4, 5 |
| 100–159 | checkerboards cell 1, 2, 4; plus a 1px yellow/red checker |
| 160–219 | Bayer ramp, black on white, ratio 0.0 → 1.0 left to right |
| 220–239 | Bayer ramp, yellow on white |
| 240–259 | Bayer ramp, red on black |
| 260–299 | rect, ellipse, two diagonal lines, filled triangle |
| corners | four single pixels at (396,296)=Red (399,296)=White (396,299)=Yellow (399,299)=Black |

Those four corner pixels are deliberate: they catch off-by-one errors, row/column
transposition, and vertical or horizontal flips, all of which otherwise produce
an image that looks broadly plausible.

### The exact dither rule

Go must reproduce this precisely or bands 160–259 will not match:

```
BAYER4 = {{ 0,  8,  2, 10},
          {12,  4, 14,  6},
          { 3, 11,  1,  9},
          {15,  7, 13,  5}}

ink if  ratio > (BAYER4[y%4][x%4] + 0.5) / 16.0  else bg
```

Note `+ 0.5`, and note the matrix is indexed `[y][x]`. Both matter.

### The packing rule

Four pixels per byte, two bits each, most-significant first:

```
byte = (p0&3)<<6 | (p1&3)<<4 | (p2&3)<<2 | (p3&3)
```

**Verified**: re-packing `conformance.idx` with this rule reproduces
`conformance.bin` exactly. The rule is confirmed against the vendor library,
not merely read off it.

### How to use these

Three checks, in increasing strength — do them in this order, because each one
localises a different bug:

1. **Render** the pattern in Go, compare your `*image.Paletted`'s `Pix` against
   `conformance.idx`. A mismatch is a *drawing* bug and the byte offset tells
   you which band.
2. **Pack** `conformance.idx` and compare against `conformance.bin`. A mismatch
   here is a *packing* bug, isolated from drawing.
3. **End to end**: render in Go, pack, compare against `conformance.bin`.

Only once (3) passes is it worth spending 25 seconds drawing it on the panel.

## 3. `golden/` — render goldens

*(Created at M4.)* PNGs produced by our own Go `render` package, for things
that cannot be compared against the vendor — anything involving text.

Regenerate with `go test ./render -update`. **Review the diff before
committing**: a golden test that is regenerated without being looked at asserts
nothing at all.

---

## 4. Regenerating

`tools/conformance.py` rebuilds the conformance set. It must run on the Pi, in
the reference venv, because it uses the real vendor library as the oracle:

```bash
scp tools/conformance.py sweeney@192.168.1.6:~/
ssh sweeney@192.168.1.6 'cd /tmp && ~/inky-trial/venv/bin/python ~/conformance.py'
scp sweeney@192.168.1.6:/tmp/conformance.* testdata/conformance/
```

It monkeypatches `_update` so **nothing touches SPI, GPIO or the panel** — it is
safe to run and takes about a second.

`tools/testcard_f_reference.py` is the four-ink Test Card F used during
bring-up. It is a *visual* reference for what the library should be capable of,
not a byte-comparable fixture (it has text in it). `--png out.png` renders it
with no hardware.

---

## 5. If a fixture and the hardware ever disagree

Trust the hardware, re-capture, and write down what changed. These files record
one board at one moment; a different board revision could legitimately differ —
`what-jd79668.bin` in particular is *our* board's serial-numbered record, not a
specification.
